title: Shiva's Tears, the Rudraksha
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hookLine: shiva opens his eyes after ages of tapas, his tears become seeds, and the seeds become beads
carry: japa: shiva's name, five syllables, bead by bead
tomorrow: what was falling from the hunter's tree?

cards: The Shiva Purana tells where these beads come from. Shiva once sat in tapas, deep and still, with his eyes closed, for a thousand years of the gods. When at last he opened his eyes, tears fell.

And where they touched the earth, trees grew, with rough brown seeds, wrinkled like tiny walnuts. Those seeds are rudraksha. Tonight, at the temple, a woman sits against a pillar with a string of them in her fingers.
Her thumb draws one bead toward her palm, her lips move, and the next bead comes.

teach.b: What moves along those beads is japa: repeating a name of God, again and again.

teach.h: JAPA: THE NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: On this night the name is usually Om Namah Shivaya.
Namah Shivaya is the Panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra: na, mah, shi, va, ya, salutation to Shiva.

You've met it this year, deep inside the Rudram, so the great Vedic hymn and the bead in a tired hand are joined by those five syllables. The Shiva Purana praises this mantra at length. Here's why it suits the night.
A long night needs something small. At ten in the evening a long hymn is easy to follow. At three in the morning it slips.
Five syllables you can still hold. Japa can be said aloud, whispered, or held silently, so it works in a loud crowd and a quiet room. And the beads do two jobs.
They keep count, so the mind doesn't have to. And they give the hand something to do, so when thoughts wander, there's a bead in your fingers, waiting.
Now put the story beside it: the beads came from Shiva's tears, and human hands pass them back to him, one name at a time.
That's why so many Hindu homes keep a mala near the shrine, and why you'll see a grandparent moving one through their fingers on a bus, in a waiting room, in front of the TV.
It's the practice that fits a crowded life: no temple, no hour needed.

teach.h: THE NAME, AND THE NEXT BEAD.
teach.b: Just the name, and the next bead.

how: On Maha Shivaratri, some who keep the vigil do japa of Om Namah Shivaya, aloud, whispered or silently, counting on a rudraksha mala, alongside temple songs and worship through the night.

games.why: japa is built for the hour when bigger things slip away: one short name, Om Namah Shivaya, on bead after bead.

practice: Choose something short to repeat, one breath at a time: Om Namah Shivaya if you pray, or a name of God from your own tradition, or simply counting breaths from one to ten.
If you have beads, or a string with knots, let the fingers move one at a time, and when you notice you've drifted, don't start over; just take the next bead, the next breath, the next word.
